analysis.one_liner: Requires Texas's isolated power grid to connect to neighboring grids, with federal backup loans.
analysis.headline: Introduced in late February 2026 with 15 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where no further action had been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: Texas runs its own power grid, separate from the rest of the country, so it cannot easily buy or sell electricity with its neighbors. This bill would end that isolation: it would put the Texas grid (ERCOT) under federal oversight like the rest of the country's grids, and it would order the construction of transmission lines connecting Texas to the nearby grids in the Plains, Midwest, and West, with a deadline of January 1, 2037 [S2]. It also increases federal loan money for transmission projects from $2.5 billion to $13.5 billion and orders a study on linking Texas to Mexico's grid [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Texans and other electricity consumers. A connected grid means Texas can import power during the kind of extreme weather that caused deadly blackouts in 2021, and export cheap wind and solar power when it has a surplus. The bill also directs that construction use prevailing wages and registered apprenticeship programs, and requires outreach to environmental justice communities and Tribes [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Strips the Texas grid's decades-old exemption from federal (FERC) jurisdiction under the Federal Power Act, making it play by the same rules as the rest of the country [S2].

Requires a new federal reliability standard setting minimum transfer capability between ERCOT and each neighboring grid — ranging up to 12.6 gigawatts toward the Plains grid, 16.2 toward the Midwest grid, and 7.9 toward the Western grid — with interconnection projects completed by January 1, 2037 [S2].
Raises the Transmission Facilitation Program's federal borrowing authority from $2.5 billion to $13.5 billion to help finance new transmission lines [S2].

Directs siting to use existing rights-of-way and degraded land, expand access to renewable energy, provide community involvement including translation and virtual attendance, and use prevailing wages and registered apprenticeship programs [S2].
Orders a study on the reliability, climate, and cost benefits of connecting Texas's grid to Mexico's [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passes, ERCOT utilities and Texas power generators lose their exemption from federal oversight, and the cost of building new transmission lines would ultimately flow through to electricity customers, though federal loans would cover part of the financing [S2].

drawbacks.text: Building thousands of miles of transmission lines is expensive, and while the bill provides $13.5 billion in federal loans, much of the cost of interconnection would end up in electric bills paid by households and businesses [S2].

The bill keeps National Environmental Policy Act and Endangered Species Act review requirements for the new projects, which supports community and environmental safeguards but adds time and cost to construction [S2].

Texas officials and ERCOT participants have long argued that their separation from federal oversight keeps costs down and state control local; stripping the exemption (sections of the Federal Power Act covering transmission siting, financing, and order enforcement) removes that autonomy [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The reliability gains are substantial: an isolated grid that failed catastrophically during the 2021 winter storm cannot easily buy emergency power, and interconnection gives Texans a backstop plus cheaper power year-round. The honest cost is money — transmission is expensive and customers pay part of it — plus the loss of Texas's exemption from federal grid oversight. On balance the bill is a clear benefit to consumers, but it has no realistic path in a Republican-controlled House where it has zero Republican cosponsors.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearings or action since.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Casar introduced the Connect the Grid Act on February 26, 2026, with 15 Democratic cosponsors [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day and has received no further action — no markup, no hearing, no floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill stuck in committee, the status quo persists: ERCOT utilities and Texas generators keep their exemption from federal oversight, and transmission construction interests wait on federal money that has not expanded.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: ERCOT utilities keep the status quo

for.name: Rep. Greg Casar
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House

for.name: 15 of 217 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Ocasio-Cortez (NY), Escobar (TX), and Garcia (TX)

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the referral; no hearings, markup, or further action on the bill has been recorded

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican support is recorded, and the Republican-chaired Energy and Commerce Committee has taken no action.

industries.industry: ERCOT utilities and Texas power generators
industries.note: The bill repeals the Texas grid's exemptions from Federal Power Act provisions on transmission siting, financing, and FERC jurisdiction, subjecting them to federal regulation for the first time since the 1930s. Their interest in staying exempt runs against a connected grid that protects consumers during emergencies.

industries.industry: Transmission construction and electric infrastructure firms
industries.note: The bill mandates new interconnection lines by 2037 and expands the Transmission Facilitation Program from $2.5 billion to $13.5 billion in federal loan authority, creating a large pipeline of construction work — with prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements directing the jobs benefit to workers.

industries.industry: Texas renewable energy producers (wind, solar, geothermal)
industries.note: Interconnection lets Texas's abundant cheap renewables reach distant markets instead of being curtailed when supply exceeds local demand, and the bill directs siting to expand renewable access.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is a first-step introduction with no Republican cosponsors in a Republican-controlled House, sitting in the Energy and Commerce Committee with no scheduled action. The overwhelming pattern for bills at this stage is to die quietly at the end of the Congress without a hearing or vote; even in the unlikely event of committee action, Senate consideration would require Republican support that is absent.
